content_voiceover: This table is a board favorite: distinguishing platelet or vessel disorders from coagulation factor disorders using history and exam. Petechiae are characteristic of platelet or vessel disorders, but rare in coagulation disorders; deep dissecting hematomas and hemarthrosis flip that, characteristic of coagulation disorders, rare with platelet problems. Superficial ecchymoses are large and solitary in coagulation disorders, small and multiple in platelet disorders. Delayed bleeding after trauma points to a coagulation factor problem, since clot formation is what's failing, not the initial platelet plug. Bleeding from superficial cuts is minimal in coagulation disorders but persistent, often profuse, in platelet disorders. Sex matters: eighty to ninety percent of inherited coagulation disorders, hemophilia A and B, are X-linked and male-only, while platelet disorders are relatively more common in females. And positive family history is common in coagulation disorders but rare in platelet disorders, except von Willebrand disease and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, the key exceptions to memorize.
keypoints: Petechiae = platelet/vessel; hemarthrosis/deep hematoma = coagulation factor
80-90% inherited coagulation d/o = X-linked males; platelet d/o more common in females
Family hx rare in platelet d/o except vWD, HHT
keypoint_voiceover: Petechiae and small multiple bruises point to platelets or vessels. Deep hematomas, hemarthrosis, large solitary bruises, and delayed bleeding point to a coagulation factor problem. Most inherited coagulation disorders are X-linked and male-only, while platelet disorders skew female. And family history is common in coagulation disorders but rare in platelet disorders, except von Willebrand disease and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.
